text: What is true about tuples? (Select two answers.)

options.text: The .append() method can be used to extend any tuple.
The del keyword can be applied to a single tuple element in order to remove it.
You can use indexing in order to get any tuple's element.
Tuples are immutable, which means that you're not allowed to change their contents.

explanation_en: The .append() method can be used to extend any tuple – False: the only outcome you may expect here is the AttributeError exception – tuples don't have the .append() method. The del keyword can be applied to a single tuple element – False: immutable beings (including tuples) can't be objects to mutate. You can use the del keyword to remove a tuple as a whole, but not to change its contents. Indexing – True: in this case tuples behave like lists. Immutability – True: it can be said that immutability is the key difference between tuples and lists.

text: What is true about tuples? (Select two answers.)

options.text: All tuple elements must be of the same type.
The phrase tuple() can be used to produce an empty tuple.
The + operator can be applied to tuples and means concatenation.
The phrase (1) describes a one-element tuple.

explanation_en: All tuple elements must be of the same type – False: tuples of that kind would be very inflexible and of little use. tuple() – True: an empty pair of parentheses () will work, too. The + operator – True: for example, (1,) + (2,) evaluates to (1, 2). Note the commas – you're not allowed to omit them! The phrase (1) – False: it's a single integer value equal to one. To make it a tuple, you need to include the comma: (1,).

text: What is the expected result of the following code?
code:
answers = (True, True, False)
selection = answers[3:]
points = 0
for answer in selection[-2:]:
    if answer:
        points += 1
print(points)
explanation_en: Note: the selection has been created as a zero-element slice of answers (the slice starts beyond the list!). The second slice (the one in the loop statement) changes nothing (the empty list remains empty), and therefore points is not incremented even once inside the loop, and its final value is 0.

text: What is the expected result of the following code?
code:
answers = (True, False, True)
selection = answers[2:]
points = 0
for answer in selection[-1:]:
    if answer:
        points += 1
print(points)
explanation_en: Note: the selection has been created as a one-element slice of the answers list. Therefore, it is a separate, one-element list which contains True. The second slice (the one in the loop statement) changes nothing (the only list element is also its last element). In effect, points is incremented once inside the loop and its final value is 1.
